title: How can a rectangle be cut into an isosceles triangle?
description: A rectangle is cut along a diagonal into two matching right triangles. One is flipped and stood back to back with the other along the leg equal to the width, and the two make an isosceles triangle of the same area.
teaching_notes: One idea: the diagonal makes two matching right triangles that join back to back as an isosceles triangle. Watch for students who join them along the diagonal instead.

source: Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 8, Sulba Sutras)
video_script.why: The child uses cut and join from the solved example to dissect a rectangle into an isosceles triangle of the same area.
video_script.substitution: Cut along a diagonal, flip one piece, and stand the two back to back.
video_script.anchor: the book's rectangle ABCD with the diagonal AC
video_script.payoff_line: Cut along a diagonal and stand the two right triangles back to back

final_answer.value: cut along a diagonal and stand the two right triangles back to back
final_answer.spoken: cut along a diagonal and stand the two right triangles back to back

maths_rules: rectangle with length l and width w; the diagonal makes two matching right triangles with legs l and w
a flipped copy joined along the legs of length w makes the two legs of length l lie in one straight line, since two right angles make a straight angle
the new triangle has base 2l and height w, and its two slanting sides are the diagonal, so it is isosceles
area = 1/2 × 2l × w = l × w, the area of the rectangle
video_script.design: One rectangle all video: one cut along the diagonal, one flip, and the pieces stand back to back.
